title: Access-A-Ride in NYC: how to qualify, book and pay
seoTitle: Access-A-Ride NYC: Eligibility, Booking and Fares
seoDesc: How Access-A-Ride paratransit works in New York City: who qualifies, the free assessment, booking by phone or MY AAR, the fare, e-hail, and options outside NYC.
dek: Access-A-Ride is the MTA's shared-ride service for New Yorkers whose disability keeps them off buses and subways. Here is how to apply, book a trip and pay, plus what's available outside the city.
keyFacts: Runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, across all five boroughs
Fare equals the full subway and bus fare ($3); a listed care attendant rides free
Book 1 to 2 days ahead, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m.: 877-337-2017, option 2
Eligibility decision within 21 days of your in-person assessment
Cancel at least two hours before pickup
body:
Access-A-Ride (AAR) is the MTA's paratransit service for New York City residents and visitors whose disability prevents them from using public buses and subways. You apply, go to a free in-person assessment, and if approved, book shared rides a day or two ahead for the same fare as a subway ride.

Age alone doesn't qualify someone. A healthy 80-year-old who can ride the bus won't be approved, while a 66-year-old with severe arthritis who can't manage stairs might be. This guide covers who qualifies, how to apply, how to book and pay, the e-hail pilot, and what's available outside the city.

Who qualifies for Access-A-Ride?

Access-A-Ride follows the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). It serves people whose disability prevents them from using buses and subways, some or all of the time. After the assessment, the MTA assigns one of these eligibility types.

Eligibility typeWhat it means
FullEligible for all trips
Temporary fullEligible for all trips for a limited time
ConditionalEligible only in certain conditions
Temporary conditionalConditional eligibility for a limited time
ContinualOngoing eligibility with no recertification, though an update form is due every 5 years
IneligibleDoes not meet the criteria

Conditional eligibility covers specific barriers. Examples include inaccessible subway stations, extreme cold (a forecast of 39°F or below), extreme heat (a forecast of 90°F or above), unfamiliar places, or a stop or station more than a set number of blocks away.

The service area is all five boroughs plus a three-quarter-mile band beyond the city line into nearby parts of Nassau and Westchester counties. It runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week, including holidays.

How do you apply?

  1. Submit an inquiry. Use the online inquiry form linked from the MTA's apply page or call 877-337-2017 and choose option 4 for eligibility (9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday to Friday).
  2. Get your packet. The MTA mails a paper application, an appointment letter and instructions for booking free round-trip transportation to the assessment.
  3. Book your ride to the assessment. It's free. Mention if a personal care attendant (PCA) will travel with you. PCAs ride free too.
  4. Bring the completed application. Assessments are held at centers in each borough, based on availability.
  5. Meet with a health care professional. The assessment includes an interview and, if appropriate, functional testing.
  6. Wait for the decision. The MTA decides within 21 days of the assessment and mails your eligibility letter.

If your parent is denied or given only conditional eligibility, they can appeal within 60 days. The appeal form and instructions come with the eligibility letter.

Full and conditional riders recertify every 5 years. If you don't get a recertification notice, contact the Eligibility Unit about six weeks before the AAR ID expires.

Helping a parent apply

Go with your mom or dad to the assessment if you can. Bring a list of medications and conditions, and be ready to describe a bad day as well as a good one. People tend to downplay their limits when a stranger is watching.

How do you book a trip?

Trips are booked one to two days in advance. Same-day trips are not available.

  • By phone. Call 877-337-2017 from the New York area, or 718-393-4999 from elsewhere. Choose your language, then option 2. Agents take reservations 7 a.m. to 5 p.m., seven days a week.
  • Online or in the app. Use MY AAR (linked from the MTA's book and manage trips page) or the MTA app, logging in with your AAR ID and password. First-time users register first.
  • By text. Send any text to 833-227-6928 to start a text session with AAR.
  • Relay. Customers who are deaf or hard of hearing can use their preferred relay service or 711.

Other phone options

On the same lines, option 1 is a 24/7 self-service system. Option 3 lets you check, cancel or ask for a later pickup on a trip booked for today, with agents available 24/7. Option 5 handles subscription service, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily. Option 6 takes feedback, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. weekdays.

Subscription trips and cancellations

If your parent goes from the same place to the same place at the same time at least once a week, such as dialysis or a day program, ask for a subscription trip. Request it at least three days before the first ride.

Cancel any trip at least two hours before pickup. To change a trip, cancel it and rebook with the new details. AAR is a shared-ride service, so trips may include other stops. Build extra time into appointments.

What does Access-A-Ride cost?

The Access-A-Ride fare matches the full subway and local bus fare, which is $3 as of the January 4, 2026 fare change. Each one-way trip is paid separately.

RiderFare
AAR customer$3, same as the full subway and bus fare
Personal care attendant noted on the AAR IDFree
Guest without the PCA notationFull AAR fare, in exact change
Fair Fares NYC participant paying with OMNYHalf fare

There are two ways to pay. Pay the driver in exact change, since drivers don't give change. Or preload money on the AAR OMNY ID card. AAR vehicles have no OMNY readers, so show the card to the driver and the fare comes off your balance at the end of the trip. Eligible customers get the AAR OMNY ID card by mail, and it also works as photo ID. It can't be used for taxi or e-hail trips.

Four free rides a day on buses and subways

Eligible AAR customers also get four free rides a day on MTA subways, local, limited and Select Bus Service buses, the Staten Island Railway and the Roosevelt Island Tram. For a parent who can manage some trips on transit, that's a real saving.

On good days, the bus or subway may be faster, and for AAR riders the first four rides each day are free.

What is the e-hail pilot?

The MTA's E-Hail Pilot Program gives some AAR customers on-demand rides through taxi and app services. It has run since 2017. Participants were selected at random, and the MTA says it is not adding customers on request.

  • The rider pays $4 per trip to start.
  • The MTA covers up to $60 of each trip, so a trip costing up to $64 costs the rider $4. The rider pays anything above that.
  • Each participant gets 25 or 40 subsidized trips per calendar month, based on past use. After that, the rider pays the full cost.
  • Providers are Arro, CTG, Lyft, Uber and the Drivers Cooperative. CTG, Uber and the Drivers Cooperative also take phone bookings.

If your parent wasn't chosen, the regular advance-booking service is the option. The MTA's page describes the current phase as starting in July 2024, so check the MTA e-hail page for the latest terms.

What mistakes trip people up?

  • Waiting until the day of. Same-day trips aren't available. Book one to two days ahead, between 7 a.m. and 5 p.m.
  • Cancelling too late. Cancel at least two hours before pickup. MY AAR and the 24/7 same-day line (option 3) make this easier, even at night.
  • Bringing the wrong money. Drivers don't make change. Carry the exact fare or keep money on the AAR OMNY ID card.
  • Bringing a helper who isn't listed. A companion rides free only if "PCA" is noted on the AAR ID. Otherwise they pay the full fare as a guest.
  • Letting eligibility lapse. Watch for the recertification notice. If it doesn't come, call the Eligibility Unit about six weeks before the ID expires.
  • Not appealing. If a denial or conditional rating doesn't match your parent's real limits, appeal within 60 days.

What about visitors and riders outside NYC?

Visitors who are paratransit-eligible where they live can use AAR for up to 21 days in a 365-day period. Contact the AAR Eligibility Unit at least 2 weeks before arriving. Documents can be faxed to 718-393-4306 or mailed to AAR Eligibility, Department of Paratransit, 130 Livingston Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201.

Outside the five boroughs and the border band, paratransit is run by local systems. In Nassau County it's NICE Able-Ride (reservations 516-228-4000). In Suffolk County it's Suffolk County Accessible Transit, or SCAT (631-853-8337). The MTA's paratransit providers page also lists services in Westchester, Rockland, Putnam, Orange and Dutchess counties. Upstate and elsewhere, ask your county's transit agency or Office for the Aging. NY Connects can point you to the right office at 1-800-342-9871.

Should your parent also get a Reduced-Fare card?

Yes, if they're 65 or older and ride buses or subways at all. MTA reduced fare is $1.50 on subways and local buses, half the $3 base fare. It's a separate program from Access-A-Ride, and there's no assessment for riders 65 and up. See our guide to MTA reduced fare in New York for how to apply.

If your parent recently stopped driving or just came home from rehab, it can help to set up both at once. Our caregiver support guide lists other help for families managing a parent's appointments.

faq.q: How do I sign my mom up for Access-A-Ride in Queens?
faq.a: Start with the MTA's online inquiry form (aar.mta.info/inquiry) or call 877-337-2017 and choose option 4. The MTA mails an application and an appointment for a free in-person assessment, with free round-trip transportation. A decision comes within 21 days of the assessment.

faq.q: Does my dad in Staten Island qualify for Access-A-Ride just because he's over 65?
faq.a: No. Access-A-Ride is based on disability, and age alone doesn't qualify anyone. He qualifies if a disability keeps him from using buses and subways some or all of the time. At 65 he does qualify for MTA reduced fare, which is a separate program.

faq.q: How much is an Access-A-Ride trip?
faq.a: The fare matches the full subway and bus fare, $3. A personal care attendant listed on the AAR ID rides free. Guests pay the full fare in exact change.

faq.q: Can I book Access-A-Ride for the same day?
faq.a: No. Trips are booked one to two days in advance, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m., by calling 877-337-2017 (option 2) or through MY AAR or the MTA app.

faq.q: Does Access-A-Ride go to Long Island or Westchester?
faq.a: Only a short way. The service area includes a three-quarter-mile band beyond the city line into nearby parts of Nassau and Westchester. Beyond that, local paratransit applies, such as NICE Able-Ride in Nassau (516-228-4000) or SCAT in Suffolk (631-853-8337).

faq.q: How do I cancel an Access-A-Ride trip?
faq.a: Cancel at least two hours before pickup through MY AAR or the MTA app, or call 877-337-2017. Choose option 2 for trips booked 1 to 2 days out (7 a.m. to 5 p.m.) or option 3 for a trip today (24/7).

sources: MTA, Apply or recertify for Access-A-Ride
MTA, Book and manage AAR trips
MTA, Paratransit providers in the region

title: New York estate tax: the 2026 exclusion, the cliff and filing
seoTitle: New York Estate Tax 2026: $7.35M Exclusion and Cliff
seoDesc: New York's 2026 estate tax exclusion is $7,350,000. How the 105% cliff works, who files Form ET-706, the nine-month deadline and the three-year gift add-back.
dek: Most New York estates owe no state estate tax, but the ones near the line need to plan carefully. Here is the 2026 exclusion amount, the cliff, and what an executor must file.
keyFacts: 2026 basic exclusion amount: $7,350,000 (deaths Jan 1 to Dec 31, 2026)
2025 basic exclusion amount: $7,160,000
No credit at all once the taxable estate tops 105% of the exclusion
File Form ET-706 and pay within nine months of death
Taxable gifts made within three years of death are added back
body:
New York's estate tax applies only when an estate is larger than the basic exclusion amount, which is $7,350,000 for people who die in 2026. Above that line the tax rises fast, and once the taxable estate passes 105% of the exclusion, tax is figured on the whole taxable estate.

That sharp jump is what planners call the New York cliff. Most families will never come close to it. But estates with a paid-off house in the city or suburbs, retirement accounts and life insurance can add up faster than people expect. This guide explains the numbers, who files, and the gift rule that surprises many families.

What is the 2026 exclusion amount?

The basic exclusion amount is the value an estate can have before New York estate tax applies. The New York State Department of Taxation and Finance publishes it by date of death.

Date of deathBasic exclusion amount
January 1 to December 31, 2026$7,350,000
January 1 to December 31, 2025$7,160,000
2027Not yet published by the Tax Department

The amount is adjusted for inflation each year. As of late November 2026, the Tax Department had not posted the 2027 figure. Check the Tax Department's estate tax page for updates.

The federal estate tax is a separate tax with its own exemption and rules.

How does the New York cliff work?

New York gives every estate a credit that wipes out the tax on estates at or below the exclusion amount. Above the exclusion, that credit shrinks quickly. When the taxable estate is more than 105% of the exclusion, the credit disappears entirely, and tax is figured on the full taxable estate.

The 105% line comes straight from the Tax Department's rule. Its Form ET-706 instructions for 2025 deaths put the cutoff at $7,518,000, which is 105% of that year's $7,160,000 exclusion. Applying the same 105% rule to the 2026 exclusion of $7,350,000 gives $7,717,500. So for 2026 deaths the credit phases out between $7,350,000 and $7,717,500, and above $7,717,500 there's no credit at all.

An example

Say your mother dies in 2026 with a taxable estate of $7,300,000. That's under the exclusion, so no New York estate tax is due. Now say it's $7,800,000. That's above $7,717,500, so the credit is gone and tax is figured on the entire $7,800,000. Going over the line by a few hundred thousand dollars brings tax on the full amount.

Date of deathExclusion amountNo credit above (105% of exclusion)
2026$7,350,000$7,717,500
2025$7,160,000$7,518,000

That's why the last few hundred thousand dollars matter so much in New York. Planners sometimes use charitable gifts in a will to bring an estate back under the line, since a smaller tax bill can leave heirs with more. Ask an estate lawyer or accountant about this if an estate is anywhere near the cliff.

Near the line, a modest charitable bequest can sometimes leave the family with more money in the end.

Who has to file a New York estate tax return?

The executor files. The rules differ for residents and nonresidents.

  • New York residents. File if the federal gross estate plus includible gifts is more than the basic exclusion amount.
  • Nonresidents. File if the estate includes real estate or tangible property located in New York, and the same total is more than the exclusion amount. A Florida retiree who kept a house in the Hudson Valley is a common example.

The return is Form ET-706. Use the version that matches the date of death. A completed federal Form 706 must be filed with it, even when the estate doesn't have to file a federal return.

  1. Value everything at date of death. Include real estate, accounts, retirement plans, life insurance the decedent owned, business interests and personal property.
  2. Add back recent gifts. Include taxable gifts made in the three years before death that are not already in the estate (see below).
  3. Compare to the exclusion. If the total is over the exclusion amount for the year of death, the estate must file.
  4. Prepare ET-706 and federal Form 706. Use the ET-706 version for the date of death. Attach the completed federal return.
  5. File and pay within nine months of death. If you need more time, request an extension on Form ET-133.
  6. Clear the lien on real estate. To sell or transfer New York real estate, you may need a Release of Lien of Estate Tax (Form ET-117) for each county where it's located. Estates that don't need to file ET-706 use Form ET-30 to apply for the release.

What is the three-year gift add-back?

Giving money away shortly before death doesn't automatically reduce a New York estate. For New York residents, taxable gifts made within three years of death are added back to the estate if they aren't already included in the federal gross estate. A taxable gift here means a gift that would be taxable under section 2503 of the Internal Revenue Code.

A few gifts are not added back.

  • Gifts made while the person was not a New York resident.
  • Gifts made before April 1, 2014.
  • Gifts made between January 1 and January 15, 2019.
  • Gifts of real or tangible property located outside New York when the gift was made.

Here's how it plays out. Say your father, a New York resident, gave his daughter $500,000 toward a home in 2025 and died in 2026. If that gift was taxable under federal gift rules and isn't already in his federal gross estate, the taxable part is added back when figuring whether his estate crosses $7,350,000 and how much New York tax is due.

In practice, this means deathbed gifting rarely helps with New York tax. Gifts made well before the three-year window are a different matter, which is one reason estate plans work best when they start early.

What counts toward the estate?

The starting point is the federal gross estate, the same figure used on federal Form 706. It generally includes what the person owned at death, valued as of the date of death. For most New York families the big pieces are the home, bank and brokerage accounts, retirement accounts and any life insurance the person owned.

Real estate is often the surprise. A house bought decades ago in Westchester, on Long Island or in Brooklyn may now be worth far more than the family thinks. Get a realistic value before deciding the estate is safely under the line. For an estate near the exclusion, a formal appraisal is worth the cost, because the cliff turns small valuation differences into large tax differences.

When is the tax due, and can you get more time?

The executor must file the New York return, the federal return and pay any tax due within nine months of the date of death. An extension to file or pay is requested on Form ET-133. Extensions generally can't be longer than six months, though the Tax Department may allow up to four years to pay in cases of undue hardship.

Estimate the tax early. If the estate is short on cash because most of its value is in a house, talk to a tax professional well before the nine-month mark.

Who pays the tax, the estate or the heirs?

New York's tax is charged on the estate itself. The executor files and pays it from the estate before heirs receive their shares. The Tax Department's instructions direct the executor to file the return and pay the tax.

Families split between states should check the other state's rules too, because each state sets its own death taxes. If a parent lived in New Jersey or another state but owned a house or land in New York, the nonresident filing rule above applies on the New York side.

Income tax is a separate question from estate tax. Our guide to how New York taxes retirement income covers the state income tax side for older adults.

Who should the executor call first?

Start with the estate's lawyer or accountant, and do it in the first month or two. The ET-706 needs a completed federal Form 706 attached, and that return takes time to prepare. Appraisals of real estate and business interests take time too. Starting early leaves room to ask for an extension on Form ET-133 if it's needed.

What should families do now?

Add up the rough value of your parent's estate, including the house, retirement accounts and any life insurance they own. If the total is well under $7 million, New York estate tax is unlikely to be a worry, though the rest of their plan still matters. Our guides to powers of attorney and probate in New York cover the paperwork every family needs.

If the total is in the $6 million to $8 million range, or growing, see an estate planning lawyer or CPA. The cliff makes small differences expensive, and the three-year add-back rules out last-minute fixes.

faq.q: What is the New York estate tax exemption for 2026?
faq.a: The basic exclusion amount is $7,350,000 for dates of death from January 1 through December 31, 2026. For 2025 deaths it was $7,160,000.

faq.q: What is the 2027 New York estate tax exclusion?
faq.a: As of late November 2026, the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance had not published the 2027 amount. Check tax.ny.gov for the update.

faq.q: Will my parents' house in Nassau County push their estate over the New York limit?
faq.a: Add the house's value to their bank and retirement accounts, life insurance they own and other assets. If the total for a 2026 death is more than $7,350,000, the estate must file Form ET-706. Above $7,717,500 (105% of the exclusion), tax applies to the whole taxable estate.

faq.q: My dad lived in Florida but owned a cabin in the Adirondacks. Does his estate owe New York tax?
faq.a: A nonresident's estate must file if it includes New York real estate or tangible property and the federal gross estate plus includible gifts is more than the exclusion amount. The Form ET-706 instructions explain how a nonresident estate's tax is figured, so ask the estate's accountant to work through them.

faq.q: When is the New York estate tax return due?
faq.a: Form ET-706, along with a completed federal Form 706, and any tax due must be filed and paid within nine months of the date of death. Extensions are requested on Form ET-133.

faq.q: Can my mom give money away to avoid New York estate tax?
faq.a: Taxable gifts made within three years of death are generally added back to a New York resident's estate. Gifts made earlier are not added back, so planning ahead matters. Talk to an estate planning lawyer before making large gifts.

sources: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance, Estate tax
NYS Tax Department, Instructions for Form ET-706
NYS Tax Department, TSB-M-14(6)M, estate tax changes

title: Home safety changes in New York: grab bars, ramps and repair help
seoTitle: Home Modifications for Seniors in NY: Grants and Help
seoDesc: RESTORE, Access to Home, NYC Aging home modifications and weatherization help older New Yorkers pay for grab bars, ramps and repairs. Who qualifies and how.
dek: Grab bars, ramps and urgent repairs can keep a parent safely at home. Here are the New York programs that help pay, who qualifies, and the low-cost changes that prevent falls.
keyFacts: RESTORE: emergency repairs for homeowners 60+ up to 100% of area median income
Access to Home: accessibility changes up to 80% of area median income
You apply through a local town, county or nonprofit, not HCR
NYC Aging Home Modification Program: 212-602-4455
Weatherization is free for eligible owners and renters; seniors get priority
body:
New York has several programs that pay for grab bars, ramps, railings and urgent repairs so older adults can stay safely at home. The main state programs are RESTORE, for emergency repairs for homeowners 60 and older, and Access to Home, for accessibility changes for people with disabilities; you apply through a local nonprofit or town, never to the state directly.

New York City adds its own options, including NYC Aging's Older Adult Home Modification Program, which installs modifications at no cost after an occupational therapist visits. Your county Office for the Aging can point you to local handyman or minor repair help, and the Weatherization Assistance Program can fix drafty, cold homes for free if income qualifies. This guide covers who qualifies for each, what they pay for, and the simple changes that prevent falls.

Which New York programs help pay for home safety changes?

The right program depends on what needs fixing, whether your parent owns or rents, and where they live. Here is a quick comparison from the official program pages.

ProgramWho qualifiesWhat it coversHow to apply
RESTORE (HCR)Homeowners 60+ living in the home, income at or below 100% of area median incomeEmergency repairs and code violations that threaten health or safetyThrough a local program administrator (town, county or nonprofit)
Access to Home (HCR)People with a documented disability, income at or below 80% of area median income; owners or rentersRamps, lifts, handrails, wider doorways, roll-in showersThrough a local program administrator
Access to Home for Medicaid Members (HCR)Medicaid members with a disability, same income limitSame kinds of accessibility changesThrough a local program administrator
NYC Aging Older Adult Home Modification ProgramEligible older New Yorkers in the five boroughsNo-cost grab bars, handrails, raised toilet seats, shower chairs, lighting, temporary ramps, non-slip flooring212-602-4455
HPD HomeFix (NYC)Owners of 1 to 4 family homes, income up to 120% of area median incomeNo-interest, forgivable repair loans, including accessibility measures for seniorsCenter for NYC Neighborhoods, 646-513-3470
Weatherization Assistance Program (HCR)Households at or below 60% of state median income; owners and rentersInsulation, air sealing, heating repairs, windows and doors, at no costLocal weatherization provider

How does the RESTORE program work?

RESTORE pays for emergency repairs for homeowners 60 and older. New York State Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) funds it, and local governments and nonprofits run it.

To qualify, HCR says your parent must own the home and live in it as a primary residence, be 60 or older, and have household income no higher than 100% of the area median income. The repair must fix a hazard or deficiency that poses an immediate threat to life, health or safety, or a code violation.

Rockland County's community development office, which runs RESTORE locally, lists common covered repairs. They include serious structural problems with floors, doorways and entry decks, leaking roofs, broken exterior doors and windows, deteriorated stairs, failed heating systems, plumbing and hot water, electrical hazards and accessibility modifications. It does not cover kitchen or bathroom remodels, landscaping, cosmetic work or new construction. Rockland also requires applicants to be current on property taxes and to carry homeowners insurance. The income chart on its page lists 100% of area median income as $118,800 for one person and $135,700 for two. Other counties have different limits.

Funding comes in rounds, so a local program can be open or closed. As of November 2026, Rockland's page says RESTORE is not accepting applications and will open again if more funding becomes available. Call 845-364-3939 to ask.

You can't apply to the state for RESTORE or Access to Home. The money goes through a local town, county or nonprofit.

What does Access to Home pay for?

Access to Home helps people with disabilities make their homes accessible, so they can stay there or come home instead of moving to a facility. HCR gives wheelchair ramps and lifts, handrails, doorway widening and roll-in showers as examples.

The person must have a documented substantial limitation caused by a disability, and household income at or below 80% of area median income. The limit is 120% for veterans certified by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs or the Department of Defense as entitled to disability payments for a wartime disability. Renters can qualify too, as long as the landlord isn't already required by law to make the changes. A separate version, Access to Home for Medicaid Members, serves people on Medicaid with the same income rule.

  1. Open HCR's local grants list. HCR posts a list of active grants by county, including RESTORE and Access to Home, on its "Grants Available Through Local Partners" page.
  2. Call the group serving your parent's area. Confirm the program is open and ask for the application and income limit.
  3. Gather documents. Expect proof of age, income, ownership or lease, and, for Access to Home, documentation of the disability.
  4. Schedule the inspection. The local administrator decides what work qualifies.
  5. Ask about other help. If no grant is open, HCR suggests contacting the town or a local housing nonprofit. Also call the county Office for the Aging.

What help is there in New York City?

NYC Aging runs the Older Adult Home Modification Program. A licensed occupational therapist visits the home, recommends changes, and a licensed contractor installs them at no cost to the older adult.

NYC Aging says modifications may include grab bars, handrails, raised toilet seats, shower chairs, better lighting, temporary ramps and non-slip flooring. It coordinates the assessment, the plan, the installation and a follow-up visit. For eligibility or to apply, call 212-602-4455 or email HomeMod@aging.nyc.gov.

Homeowners can also look at HPD's HomeFix program. It offers no-interest, forgivable loans for repairs to one to four family homes, up to $100,000 for a one-family home. Eligible repairs can include roofs, heating, plumbing, electrical work and accessibility measures to help seniors. HomeFix requires the home to be the owner's primary residence, no reverse mortgage, and household income no more than 120% of area median income, which HPD lists as $142,560 for one person and $162,840 for two. Condos and co-ops are not eligible. Call the Center for NYC Neighborhoods Homeowner Hub at 646-513-3470.

Renters in the city should start with the landlord, and with NYC Aging's Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 for help.

What can my county Office for the Aging do?

Many county offices fund or refer to minor home repair and handyman programs. What exists depends on the county, so call and ask by name for "minor home repair" or "residential repair."

  • Rockland County. The Office for the Aging lists CHORE, minor home repairs for adults 60 and older or people with disabilities, sponsored by BRiDGES at 845-624-1366 ext. 139. See the Rockland County page.
  • Suffolk County. The Office for the Aging says each of the ten towns has a Residential Repair program for small jobs around the house. Participants pay for materials. Examples include Babylon 631-789-3309, Brookhaven 631-451-9092, Huntington 631-446-3721, Islip 631-224-5424 and Smithtown 631-360-7616. See the Suffolk County page.
  • Other counties. Find the local number on your county page, or call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871.

In 2022, NYSOFA began training county case managers as Certified Aging-in-Place Specialists, so they can assess a home and recommend changes. If your parent needs in-home help too, ask about EISEP, and see our NY Connects guide.

Can weatherization make an older home safer and cheaper to heat?

Yes. The Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP) improves energy efficiency and fixes energy-related health and safety problems at no cost to eligible homeowners and renters.

HCR says households may qualify with income at or below 60% of state median income, and seniors get priority. If anyone in the home gets SSI, public assistance or HEAP, the household is automatically eligible. Work starts with an energy audit and can include air sealing, attic or wall insulation, heating system repair or replacement, efficient lighting and appliances, window and door repair, and small repairs needed for energy savings. Owners of rental buildings must contribute to the cost.

To apply, contact the weatherization provider for your county, listed in HCR's online provider directory. For general questions, the WAP central office is 518-474-5700. If heating bills are the bigger worry, see our HEAP guide.

What simple changes help prevent falls?

The New York State Department of Health says falls are the leading cause of injury deaths, hospitalizations and emergency visits among adults 65 and older, and that falls are preventable. Many of its home tips cost little or nothing.

  • Remove papers, books, clothes and shoes from stairs and walkways.
  • Remove small throw rugs, or use double-sided tape so they don't slip.
  • Keep items used often in cabinets that can be reached without a step stool.
  • Have grab bars put in next to the toilet and in the tub or shower.
  • Use non-slip mats in the tub and on shower floors.
  • Brighten the lighting, and hang light curtains or shades to cut glare.
  • Have handrails and lights put in on all staircases.
  • Wear shoes inside and out, and avoid going barefoot or wearing slippers without grip.

The Department of Health also advises a yearly eye exam, a yearly foot check, and a medicine review with a doctor or pharmacist, since some medicines cause dizziness. It supports free evidence-based classes, including Tai Chi for Arthritis and Fall Prevention, A Matter of Balance and Stepping On. To find one nearby, call 518-402-7900, or ask at a senior center.

After a fall or hospital stay

Ask the hospital or rehab team whether an occupational therapist can assess the home before discharge. Then call the programs above.

What mistakes should you avoid?

  • Paying a stranger up front. Several programs above, including NYC Aging and HomeFix, arrange their own licensed or approved contractors. Be wary of anyone who knocks on the door offering repairs.
  • Waiting for one program. Funding opens and closes. Apply where you can and keep a list of others to call.
  • Skipping the renter options. Access to Home and weatherization can help renters, not just owners.

If the home simply can't be made safe, see our senior housing guide for other options.

faq.q: How do I get grab bars installed for my mom in Queens?
faq.a: Call NYC Aging's Older Adult Home Modification Program at 212-602-4455 or email HomeMod@aging.nyc.gov. For eligible older adults, a licensed occupational therapist assesses the home and a licensed contractor installs changes such as grab bars, handrails and shower chairs at no cost.

faq.q: Is there help paying for a wheelchair ramp for my dad in Westchester?
faq.a: Possibly, through New York's Access to Home program, for people with a documented disability and household income at or below 80% of area median income. Check HCR's list of active local grants by county for a Westchester administrator, and call the county Department of Senior Programs and Services.

faq.q: Who qualifies for the RESTORE program in New York?
faq.a: Homeowners 60 and older who live in the home as their primary residence and have household income at or below 100% of the area median income. The repair must fix an emergency or code violation that threatens health or safety. Apply through a local program administrator, not HCR.

faq.q: Can renters get accessibility modifications in New York?
faq.a: Yes. Access to Home can assist rental units, as long as the landlord isn't already required by law to make the changes. Renters can also apply for free weatherization. In NYC, the NYC Aging Home Modification Program serves eligible older adults.

faq.q: Does weatherization cost anything for seniors in New York?
faq.a: No. HCR says there is no cost to eligible homeowners and renters. Households at or below 60% of state median income may qualify, seniors get priority, and anyone receiving SSI, public assistance or HEAP is automatically eligible. Owners of rental buildings pay part of the cost.

faq.q: What are the cheapest ways to prevent falls at home?
faq.a: The NYS Department of Health suggests clearing clutter from stairs and walkways, removing or taping down throw rugs, using non-slip mats in the tub, improving lighting, keeping everyday items within reach, and installing grab bars and stair handrails. It also recommends yearly eye exams and a medicine review.

sources: HCR: Access to Home for Medicaid Members
HCR: Grants Available Through Local Partners
Rockland County Office for the Aging
NYC Aging: Housing Support (Older Adult Home Modification Program)
Suffolk County Office for the Aging: How Do I?
NYS Department of Health: Older Adult Fall Prevention
NYS Department of Health: Older Adults, Stay Steady, Stay Strong

title: Probate in New York: Surrogate's Court steps, fees and timing
seoTitle: Probate in New York: Steps, Fees and Small Estates
seoDesc: How probate works in New York's Surrogate's Court: when a will must be probated, the $50,000 small estate route, administration without a will, fees and timing.
dek: When a parent dies in New York, their property usually passes through the Surrogate's Court. Here is which proceeding you need, what to file, what the court charges and how long creditors have.
keyFacts: Estates are handled by the Surrogate's Court in the county of primary residence
Small estate route: personal property of $50,000 or less
Small estate filing fee: $1
Probate and administration fees run from $45 to $1,250 by estate value
Creditors generally have 7 months from when letters are first issued
body:
Probate in New York is the Surrogate's Court process that confirms a will is valid and appoints the executor to settle the estate. If there's no will, the court runs an administration proceeding instead, and if the person left $50,000 or less in personal property, a simpler small estate process may apply.

Every county in New York has a Surrogate's Court, including each of the five boroughs. You file in the county where the person who died had their primary residence. This guide walks through which proceeding fits, the steps, the court fees and how long it tends to take.

Which proceeding do you need?

The court uses a few terms you'll hear often. The person who died is the decedent. Their property is the estate. The close relatives who would inherit under state law are the distributees. The person named in the will to settle the estate is the executor.

SituationProceeding
Left a will, more than $50,000 in personal property, or real estate in their name aloneProbate
No will, more than $50,000 in personal property, or real estate in their name aloneAdministration
Personal property of $50,000 or less, with or without a willSmall estate (voluntary administration)
A wrongful death or other lawsuit may followProbate or administration, even if the estate is small

Personal property means things other than real estate, such as cash, bank accounts, stocks, bonds, cars and artwork. Real property means houses and land.

What usually passes outside probate?

Some assets go straight to a named person and never enter the estate. Common examples are accounts with a named beneficiary, such as life insurance, retirement accounts and payable-on-death bank accounts, plus property held jointly with a right of survivorship. Check each account's paperwork. These assets often make an estate small enough for the simpler process, or leave nothing to probate at all.

When does a will have to be probated?

If your parent left a will and owned property that passes under it, the original will must be filed with the Surrogate's Court and admitted to probate. Until the court admits the will and appoints the executor, nobody has legal authority to collect and distribute those assets.

Whoever holds the original will should keep it safe and unaltered. The court needs the original itself.

  1. Gather documents. Get the original will and a certified death certificate. Make a list of assets and debts.
  2. Identify everyone with a stake. List all distributees and every beneficiary named in the will, with addresses.
  3. File the probate petition. File it with the original will, the death certificate and supporting papers in the Surrogate's Court of your parent's county. Some counties accept filing online through NYSCEF, the state's electronic filing system.
  4. Get waivers or serve citations. Each distributee must be served with a notice called a citation, or sign a waiver and consent to the executor's appointment.
  5. Notify beneficiaries. Beneficiaries who inherit under the will must be officially told about the proceeding.
  6. The court admits the will. Once the Surrogate is satisfied the will is valid, the executor is appointed and can begin settling the estate.

A distributee who disagrees can appear in court and object. Objections slow everything down, so it helps to talk with family early about what the will says.

What is the small estate route?

New York's small estate process is called voluntary administration. It applies when the decedent's personal property has a gross value of $50,000 or less, with or without a will. Certain property set aside for the surviving family under state law isn't counted toward that limit.

What should you bring?

  • A certified copy of the death certificate.
  • The original will, if there is one.
  • A list of personal property with rough values: bank accounts, stocks, bonds, cars.
  • Names and addresses of the closest relatives.

Real estate changes the picture. If your parent owned a house or land in their name alone, the estate isn't small, and you need probate or administration. If the real estate was owned jointly with someone else, it can still be a small estate.

The court appoints a voluntary administrator. That's the executor if there's a will, or the closest distributee if there isn't. You file a small estate affidavit petition with a certified death certificate, plus the original will if there is one. The filing fee is $1. The courts' free Small Estate DIY program builds the forms for you, step by step.

Start with a list of every account and who it names. That one list tells you which court process you need.

What happens when there's no will?

If your parent died without a will, an administration proceeding lets the court appoint an administrator. Usually the closest family member files. The court then issues letters of administration, which give that person authority to collect and distribute the property according to law.

To start, gather a copy of the paid funeral bill and a certified death certificate. List your parent's debts and assets. Then file a petition for letters of administration in the Surrogate's Court, naming every distributee. Each distributee is served with a citation, or signs a waiver and consent.

Real estate works differently when there's no will. Under New York law, real property passes to the distributees at death. Depending on who survives, a court proceeding may not be needed just for the house. The courts suggest talking with a real estate attorney and the local tax office about how to handle the title.

In New York City, each borough is its own county with its own Surrogate's Court. So a parent who lived in Flushing files in Queens County Surrogate's Court, and one who lived in Park Slope files in Kings County (Brooklyn). The courts' online Court Locator lists addresses for every county.

Who inherits without a will?

New York's intestacy law, Estates, Powers and Trusts Law section 4-1.1, sets the order.

  • Spouse and children. The spouse gets $50,000 plus half of the rest. The children share the remainder.
  • Spouse, no children. The spouse gets everything.
  • Children, no spouse. The children share everything. A child who died earlier is represented by their own children.
  • No spouse or children. Surviving parents inherit. If none, brothers and sisters and their descendants inherit.

What does probate cost in New York?

The court's filing fee for probate or administration depends on the value of the estate. The schedule is set in section 2402 of the Surrogate's Court Procedure Act.

Estate valueFiling fee
Under $10,000$45
$10,000 to under $20,000$75
$20,000 to under $50,000$215
$50,000 to under $100,000$280
$100,000 to under $250,000$420
$250,000 to under $500,000$625
$500,000 and over$1,250
Small estate (voluntary administration)$1

Other costs can include certified copies, a bond if the will or the court requires one, and lawyers' fees. Many people handle simple estates on their own, and the courts offer DIY forms and a free Ask a Law Librarian service. A lawyer is worth considering when the will is unclear, a family member objects, there's a business or out-of-state property, or the estate may owe New York estate tax.

How long does probate take?

No official timeline applies to every estate. A simple, uncontested case where every distributee signs a waiver moves faster than one where citations must be served or someone objects.

One date matters for nearly every estate. Under Surrogate's Court Procedure Act section 1802, creditors generally have 7 months from the date letters are first issued to present claims. An executor who pays debts and distributions in good faith before a late claim arrives isn't personally liable for those payments. Even so, many executors wait out the 7 months before making final distributions so that bills can be paid first.

After that, the executor or administrator collects assets, pays valid debts and taxes, sells or transfers property, and distributes what's left. Keep a clear record of every dollar in and out.

What mistakes should families avoid?

  • Spending estate money before appointment. Until letters are issued, nobody has authority over estate accounts. A power of attorney ends at death and can't be used.
  • Mixing money. Open a separate estate account once appointed. Don't run estate money through your own account.
  • Forgetting the house. A house in your parent's name alone needs probate or administration even if the bank accounts are small.
  • Losing the original will. A copy usually isn't enough. Keep the original safe from the start.
  • Paying heirs first. Pay valid debts and taxes before distributions, and keep receipts.

If the estate is large, read our guide to New York estate tax early, since that return is due nine months after death. The power of attorney guide explains why those papers stop working at death.

faq.q: Do I have to probate my mom's will in Queens if she only had a bank account?
faq.a: It depends on the account. If the account named a beneficiary or was joint with survivorship, it may pass outside probate. If it was in her name alone and worth $50,000 or less, and she owned no real estate in her name alone, you can likely use the small estate process in Queens County Surrogate's Court for a $1 filing fee.

faq.q: How do I handle my dad's estate in Albany if he had no will?
faq.a: File a petition for letters of administration in the Albany County Surrogate's Court, naming all distributees and attaching a certified death certificate and a copy of the paid funeral bill. If his personal property was $50,000 or less and he owned no real estate in his name alone, the small estate process may apply instead.

faq.q: What is the small estate limit in New York?
faq.a: Personal property with a gross value of $50,000 or less, not counting certain property set aside for the family under state law. Real estate in the decedent's name alone takes the estate out of the small estate process.

faq.q: How much does probate cost in New York?
faq.a: The court's filing fee ranges from $45 for estates under $10,000 to $1,250 for estates of $500,000 or more. A small estate costs $1 to file. Lawyer fees, bonds and certified copies are extra.

faq.q: How long do creditors have to file claims against a New York estate?
faq.a: Generally 7 months from the date letters are first issued to an executor or administrator. A fiduciary who pays lawful claims and distributions in good faith before a late claim arrives is not personally liable for those payments.

faq.q: Can I file probate papers online in New York?
faq.a: In some counties, yes, through NYSCEF, the New York State Courts Electronic Filing system. Check the courts' e-filing county list or call your county's Surrogate's Court.

title: MTA reduced fare for 65+: half-price subway, bus and train rides
seoTitle: MTA Reduced Fare for Seniors 65+: How to Apply
seoDesc: New Yorkers 65 and older pay $1.50 on MTA subways and buses with a Reduced-Fare OMNY card. How to apply, LIRR and Metro-North discounts, upstate senior fares.
dek: At 65, New Yorkers can ride MTA subways and local buses for half price and get up to half off on the commuter railroads. Here is how to get the Reduced-Fare OMNY card, and what other New York transit systems offer.
keyFacts: Riders 65+ pay $1.50 on subways and local buses, half the $3 base fare
Express bus: $3.60, except weekday peak hours
LIRR and Metro-North: up to 50% off the one-way peak fare
After 12 paid rides in seven days with OMNY, the rest of the week is free
OMNY customer service: 877-789-6669, 24/7
body:
New Yorkers 65 and older qualify for MTA reduced fare, which cuts the subway and local bus fare to $1.50, half the $3 base fare. You apply once for a Reduced-Fare OMNY card, in person or by mail, and riders 65 and up can often get the card the same day at an MTA Customer Service Center.

The discount also applies on the Staten Island Railway, Select Bus Service and express buses outside rush hour, and up to half off on the Long Island Rail Road (LIRR) and Metro-North. This guide covers how to apply, what to bring, how the discount works on each service, and senior fares on other New York transit systems.

Who qualifies for MTA reduced fare?

Anyone 65 or older qualifies on age alone. No income test applies.

People under 65 can qualify with a disability. That includes people receiving Medicare benefits for a reason other than age, and people with serious mental illness who receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI). They use a separate disability application.

What if your parent is under 65?

A spouse or parent under 65 may still qualify through the disability route. Someone who gets Medicare because of a disability, rather than age, meets the test. So does someone with serious mental illness who receives SSI. Other qualifying disabilities are listed on the MTA's disability application.

The disability application is a separate form. By mail, include the same photo and ID as the age application, plus documentation of the disability. In person, Customer Service Center staff can help, though disability applications are more likely to need further review than a simple age application.

Reduced fare is different from Access-A-Ride. Access-A-Ride is door-to-door paratransit for people whose disability keeps them off buses and subways. If that fits your parent, see our Access-A-Ride guide.

How much do you save?

ServiceFull fareReduced fare
Subway, Staten Island Railway$3$1.50, at all times
Local, limited and Select Bus Service$3$1.50, at all times
Express bus$7.25$3.60, except weekdays 6 to 10 a.m. and 3 to 7 p.m.
LIRR and Metro-NorthVaries by tripUp to 50% off the one-way peak fare, with morning peak limits

OMNY also caps what you pay. With a Reduced-Fare OMNY card, once you've paid for 12 rides in seven days, the rest of your rides that week are free. Free transfers between buses and subways still work, as they did with MetroCard.

For a parent who rides every day, the weekly cap means a busy week of errands costs no more than 12 half-price rides.

How do you apply?

The online application is not available right now. You can apply in person or by mail.

In person (fastest)

Visit an MTA Customer Service Center at select accessible subway stations, the office at 3 Stone Street in Lower Manhattan (weekdays), or an MTA Mobile Sales van. Applicants 65 and older can often walk out with the card the same day, though some applications need more review.

By mail

  1. Get the age application. There are separate forms for age and for disability. Use the one for riders 65 and older.
  2. Add a photo. Include a passport-style photo, 2 by 1.5 inches.
  3. Copy your ID. Include a copy of a valid ID that shows your date of birth (see the list below).
  4. Mail it. Send everything to MTA New York City Transit, Attn: Reduced Fare Program, 130 Livingston St, Brooklyn, NY 11201-9625.
  5. Allow time. The MTA says new mail applicants may wait up to three months for the card.
  6. Set up the card. When it arrives, load money on it online with a free OMNY account.

What ID is accepted?

  • A valid driver's license from any state
  • A valid passport from any country
  • An IDNYC card
  • A valid state photo ID
  • A birth certificate or Medicare card, each paired with a photo ID

A Medicare card on its own isn't enough for the application. Pair it with a photo ID.

Helping a parent who doesn't use the internet

Go with them to a Customer Service Center. You'll skip the mail wait, and they can often leave with a working card. Ask the agent to show you both how to tap and how to add money.

What does that look like in a real week?

Say your mom takes the bus to the senior center and back three days a week, plus four other trips for shopping and appointments. That's 10 rides. At full fare she'd pay $30. With reduced fare she pays $15. Because of the 12-ride weekly cap, the most she can pay for subway and local bus rides in any seven days is $18, no matter how often she rides.

What mistakes should you avoid?

  • Waiting for the online form. It isn't available right now. Apply in person or by mail.
  • Sending a Medicare card alone. It counts as ID only with a photo ID.
  • Using the wrong form. There are separate applications for age and disability. Riders 65 and older use the age form.
  • Taking an express bus at rush hour. The $3.60 reduced express fare doesn't apply weekdays from 6 to 10 a.m. and 3 to 7 p.m.
  • Buying a multi-trip rail ticket. Reduced fare on the LIRR and Metro-North is sold as one-way tickets only.

How does the discount work on the LIRR and Metro-North?

Riders 65 and older pay half of the one-way peak fare on the LIRR and Metro-North. There are morning rush limits.

  • LIRR. Reduced-fare tickets can't be used on weekday morning peak trains arriving at Penn Station, Grand Central, Atlantic Terminal, Hunterspoint Avenue or Long Island City between 6 and 10 a.m.
  • Metro-North. Reduced-fare tickets can't be used on weekday morning peak trains arriving at Grand Central between 6 and 10 a.m.
  • Evening peak trains are fine on both railroads.
  • Multi-trip tickets have no reduced-fare version.

If your parent has a morning appointment in Manhattan, plan a train that arrives before 6 a.m. or after 10 a.m., or pay the regular fare for that one ride. The trip home in the afternoon or evening can use a reduced-fare ticket, even at rush hour.

Reduced-fare tickets are sold at ticket offices and on the train. Be ready to show one form of ID. The railroads accept a Reduced-Fare OMNY card or MetroCard (it doesn't need money on it), a paratransit card such as Access-A-Ride, Able-Ride or SCAT, a Medicare card, or a driver's license, birth certificate or passport showing you're over 65. A Medicaid card is not accepted.

What do other New York transit systems charge seniors?

Outside the MTA area, each region runs its own buses. Federal rules say transit systems that get federal money can charge seniors, people with disabilities and Medicare cardholders no more than half the peak fare during off-peak hours on fixed routes. Here's what three of the larger systems say.

SystemAreaSenior rule
NFTA-MetroBuffalo and Niagara FallsHalf fare for riders 65 and older, all day, with an NFTA reduced-fare card ($2). Call 716-855-6611.
CDTACapital RegionHalf-fare passes and reduced cash fares for riders 65 and older. A Medicare card can be used instead of a CDTA reduced-fare card on regularly scheduled buses. Call 518-482-8822.
CentroSyracuse and Central New YorkHalf fare for riders 65 and older with a Centro reduced-fare photo ID, or a Medicare card plus photo ID. Call 315-442-3400.

For NFTA, download the Reduced Fare Application from the NFTA website. Photos are taken at the Metropolitan Transportation Center, 181 Ellicott Street in Buffalo, weekdays 7 a.m. to 5 p.m., or at the Portage Road Transportation Center in Niagara Falls by appointment. For Centro, visit a Centro office with a photo ID and proof of birth date. The processing fee is $2, cash only.

For CDTA, reduced-fare ID cards are issued by the county Departments for the Aging in Albany, Schenectady and Saratoga counties, with a one-time $3 fee.

For other counties, call your county's transit system or Office for the Aging. NY Connects can help you find them at 1-800-342-9871.

Where can you get help with your card?

For OMNY card problems, call OMNY customer service at 877-789-6669, 24 hours a day. For Reduced-Fare MetroCard questions, call 511 and say "MTA," then "Subway and Buses." Relay users can call 711.

Transit savings add up, but they're one piece of a budget. If your parent is on a fixed income, our guide to free and discounted programs in New York lists other ways to save, and the Medicare Savings Program guide may help with health costs.

faq.q: How do I get my dad a senior MetroCard in Manhattan?
faq.a: The MTA now issues a Reduced-Fare OMNY card instead. Take him to an MTA Customer Service Center or the office at 3 Stone Street in Lower Manhattan with a valid photo ID. Riders 65 and older can often get the card the same day.

faq.q: How much is the subway for seniors in NYC?
faq.a: Riders 65 and older pay $1.50 on subways and local buses, half the $3 base fare. After 12 paid rides in seven days on a Reduced-Fare OMNY card, the rest of that week's rides are free.

faq.q: Can my mom in Westchester use her Medicare card for a discount on Metro-North?
faq.a: Yes. A Medicare card is one of the IDs Metro-North accepts for a reduced-fare ticket, which is half the one-way peak fare. Reduced-fare tickets can't be used on weekday trains arriving at Grand Central between 6 and 10 a.m.

faq.q: How long does it take to get a Reduced-Fare OMNY card by mail?
faq.a: The MTA says new mail applicants may wait up to three months. Applying in person is faster, and riders 65 and older can often get the card the same day.

faq.q: Can I apply for MTA reduced fare online?
faq.a: Not right now. The MTA says the online application is not available. Apply in person at a Customer Service Center or Mobile Sales van, or by mail to MTA New York City Transit, Attn: Reduced Fare Program, 130 Livingston St, Brooklyn, NY 11201-9625.

faq.q: Do seniors get a discount on LIRR?
faq.a: Yes. Riders 65 and older pay half the one-way peak fare. The discount isn't valid on weekday morning peak trains arriving at Penn Station, Grand Central, Atlantic Terminal, Hunterspoint Avenue or Long Island City between 6 and 10 a.m.

sources: Federal Transit Administration, reduced fares for seniors and Medicare cardholders
CDTA, Senior citizens and persons with disabilities
Centro, Half fares, passes and ID cards

title: Affordable senior housing in New York: how to apply and where
seoTitle: Affordable Senior Housing in New York: How to Apply
seoDesc: Section 202, NYCHA senior buildings, Section 8 and NYC Housing Connect lotteries for New Yorkers 62+. Who qualifies, what rent costs and how to apply.
dek: Low-cost senior apartments in New York come with income limits and long waiting lists. Here is how Section 202, NYCHA, Section 8, Housing Connect and state-financed housing work, and how to get on the lists.
keyFacts: Section 202 serves very low-income households with someone 62+
NYCHA senior buildings: everyone in the household must be 62+
NYCHA rent is 30% of gross income minus deductions
NYCHA and HCR never charge a fee to apply
NYCHA Customer Contact Center: 718-707-7771
body:
Affordable senior housing in New York comes from a handful of public programs: HUD Section 202 buildings for very low-income households with someone 62 or older, NYCHA senior buildings and Section 8 vouchers, NYC Housing Connect lotteries, and state-financed apartments you can search on the HCR website. Most have income limits, and most have waiting lists, so the single most useful step is to apply to several at once.

In most of these programs the tenant pays about 30% of income toward rent. This guide covers who qualifies for each one, how to apply in New York City and the rest of the state, how 55+ communities differ from assisted living, and how to keep rent and taxes down if your parent stays put.

What kinds of affordable senior housing are there in New York?

There are two broad kinds of help. Some programs fund whole buildings, and you apply to the building or its waiting list. Others give the renter a voucher to use with a private landlord.

ProgramWho it servesWhat the tenant paysWhere to apply
HUD Section 202Very low-income households with at least one person 62+Typically 30% of adjusted incomeEach property's owner or manager
NYCHA senior public housingHead or co-head 62+, and all other household members 62+30% of gross income minus deductionsNYCHA self-service portal or 718-707-7771
Section 8 Housing Choice VoucherLow-income households; older adults get a preference on many listsRoughly 30% of income, plus utilitiesNYCHA or HPD in NYC; HCR and its local administrators statewide
NYC Housing Connect lotteriesVaries by building; some lotteries are for applicants 62+Set rent, or 30% of income in some senior buildingsNYC Housing Connect
HCR-financed and Mitchell-Lama housingIncome-limited households; Mitchell-Lama serves middle-income families and seniorsSet by each propertyHousingSearch.ny.gov; in NYC, Mitchell-Lama lists are on NYC Mitchell-Lama Connect

What is HUD Section 202 housing?

Section 202 is a federal program that funds nonprofits to build and run apartment buildings for very low-income people 62 and older. HUD says at least one adult in the household must be 62 or older, and household income must be less than 50% of the area median income (AMI) where the property is.

HUD says residents are typically charged 30% of their adjusted income for rent, and the building receives a Project Rental Assistance Contract that covers reasonable operating costs beyond the tenant's portion. They usually include a service coordinator who links residents to community supports such as cleaning, cooking and transportation, so people can keep living on their own.

There is no single Section 202 application. HUD does not manage leasing, so you apply with each property's owner or manager directly. HUD's online Resource Locator has a search for affordable senior and special needs housing that shows 202 properties near you. Your county Office for the Aging, or NYC Aging's Aging Connect at 212-244-6469, can also help you find senior buildings nearby. Suffolk County's Office for the Aging, for example, keeps a list of federally subsidized housing in the county and notes that waiting lists can be quite long.

Put your parent on several building waiting lists at once. Each list moves on its own.

How do NYCHA senior buildings and Section 8 work in New York City?

NYCHA runs public housing for seniors where the head or co-head of household is at least 62 and everyone else in the household is 62 or older too. Rent is 30% of the household's expected gross annual income, minus deductions, and utilities are included in most buildings.

You apply online at NYCHA's self-service portal (selfserve.nycha.info). If you don't have internet, you can schedule an appointment at a NYCHA walk-in center and use a kiosk, or call the Customer Contact Center at 718-707-7771, weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. You don't submit documents with the application. They are checked later, at an eligibility interview.

A few rules from NYCHA's applicant FAQ are worth knowing:

  • No specific building. You pick a first and second choice of borough, not a development.
  • No minimum income. There is a maximum. The current public housing limit is $95,000 for one person and $108,600 for two.
  • Renew every two years. Your application stays active for 24 months. Renew it on the portal to keep your place, and you keep your original filing date.
  • No estimate of wait time. NYCHA says the waitlist is so large, and vacancies so low, that it can't estimate when you will be called.
  • Accessible apartments exist. NYCHA has 504 apartments for people with mobility impairments or special medical needs.

NYCHA also runs the largest Section 8 program in the country. With a voucher, the household generally pays 30% of adjusted monthly income toward rent and NYCHA pays the rest to the landlord. NYCHA's current Section 8 income limits are $56,700 for one person and $64,800 for two. On NYCHA's Section 8 waitlist, people 62 and older and people with disabilities are the second priority group, after people with mobility impairments living in inaccessible housing. HPD and HCR also run Section 8 programs in the city.

NYCHA warns that it never charges a fee to apply for public housing or Section 8. If someone asks your parent to pay, report it to the NYCHA Inspector General at 212-306-3355.

How do NYC Housing Connect lotteries work for older adults?

NYC Housing Connect is the city's portal for affordable rentals and homeownership across the five boroughs. You register once, then apply to individual lotteries, and applicants are drawn by lottery.

Some lotteries are only for older adults. One past example, a Mitchell-Lama lottery at Manhattan Plaza that closed on December 15, 2025, required applicants to be at least 62 and live in Community Board 4, with rent set at 30% of adjusted household income. Each listing shows the income range, household size and any preferences, such as for people who live in the local community board.

  1. Register. Create a NYC Housing Connect account with your parent's household details and income.
  2. Filter for senior listings. Search by borough, income and household size, and look for 62+ set-asides.
  3. Apply only once per lottery. Duplicate applications can disqualify you. Don't send both a paper and an online entry.
  4. Watch for alerts. Housing Connect sends deadline alerts and lets you upload documents electronically.
  5. Prepare documents. If selected, your parent will need proof of identity, household size and income at an eligibility review.
  6. Keep applying. Each lottery is separate. Applying to many raises the odds.

If the online system is hard to use, the Housing Connect applicant hotline is 212-863-7990. HPD says to leave a voicemail and the team will call back. The Housing Connect listing we checked charged no deposit or application fee. Never pay anyone to enter a lottery.

What about senior housing outside New York City?

Outside the five boroughs, start with two places: HCR's housing search website and the Section 8 office for your county. Then ask the county Office for the Aging for a list of senior buildings.

HousingSearch.ny.gov. New York State Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) runs this free site for affordable housing financed by HCR and its public and private partners. You can filter by location, rent, unit size and amenities, create one profile, and apply to properties online.

Section 8 through HCR. HCR runs the Housing Choice Voucher program through local administrators, usually by county. You can apply online through the MyHousing Portal when a waiting list is open, or on paper with your local administrator. HCR's preferences include households with an older adult or a person with a disability, as HUD defines them, among other groups. A tenant-based voucher usually has to be used within that program's area, often the county line. Being on a NYCHA or HPD list does not put you on an HCR list. You must apply separately. For help, HCR's call center is 833-791-2748.

A few local administrators near New Jersey, from HCR's list:

  • Rockland: Rockland County Department of Social Services, Pomona, 845-364-3330
  • Westchester: CVR New York Westchester HCVP, White Plains, applicant inquiries 914-873-1045
  • Orange: PathStone, Middletown, 845-343-0771
  • Putnam: Putnam County Housing Corporation, Carmel, 845-225-8493
  • Nassau and Suffolk: Community Development Long Island, Melville, 631-471-1215

Many cities and towns also have their own housing authorities with senior buildings. Those keep separate lists, so call them directly.

How is a 55+ community different from assisted living?

A 55+ community is ordinary housing with an age rule. Assisted living is licensed by the state and comes with meals, personal care and supervision.

The federal Fair Housing Act lets qualifying housing for older persons limit residents by age. Housing for people 62 and older must be intended for, and solely occupied by, people 62 or older. For a 55+ community, at least 80% of units must have at least one occupant 55 or older, the community must publish and follow policies showing it intends to be 55+ housing, and it must verify residents' ages under HUD rules. A 55+ community does not have to offer any care at all.

New York's adult care facilities are different. They are licensed by the state and overseen by the Department of Health. NYC311 describes the main types this way:

  • Adult homes provide three meals a day, housekeeping, personal care, social activities and 24-hour supervision, but not nursing care.
  • Enriched housing programs are apartments, mainly for people 65 and older, with one or two daily group meals, light personal care, housekeeping, shopping help and care management.
  • Assisted Living Programs add home health aide services, intermittent nursing and therapy for eligible residents of certain licensed adult homes or enriched housing.

You can compare licensed facilities on NYS Health Profiles, or browse them by county in our care directory. For complaints about an adult care facility, the Department of Health's intake line is 1-866-893-6772. If your parent needs nursing care around the clock, see our nursing home ratings guide.

What if my parent wants to stay where they are?

Staying put is often the cheapest choice, and several programs help with that. Renters in rent-stabilized apartments may qualify for a rent freeze, and homeowners can cut property taxes.

  • Rent freeze (NYC). NYC Aging says SCRIE can freeze rent for heads of household 62 and older with household income of $50,000 or less whose rent is more than one-third of income. See our SCRIE and DRIE guide.
  • Property tax help. See the senior citizens homeowners exemption and Enhanced STAR.
  • Eviction help (NYC). NYC Aging's Tenancy and Eviction Support Services helps older adults facing eviction in Manhattan, Brooklyn or Bronx housing court. Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469.
  • Safety changes at home. Grab bars, ramps and repairs can make a home workable for years longer. See our home modifications guide.

What mistakes should you avoid?

  • Applying to just one list. NYCHA, HPD, HCR and each Section 202 building keep separate lists.
  • Letting an application lapse. Update the address and phone number whenever they change, and renew NYCHA every two years.
  • Paying anyone to apply. NYCHA and HCR never charge application fees.
  • Confusing "senior housing" with care. A 55+ building has no aides. Ask what services, if any, come with the rent.

faq.q: How do I get my mom on a waiting list for senior housing in Brooklyn?
faq.a: Apply to several programs at once. File a NYCHA public housing application online at selfserve.nycha.info (or call 718-707-7771 for a paper one), register on NYC Housing Connect and apply to lotteries with 62+ set-asides, and contact Section 202 buildings in Brooklyn directly. Each list is separate.

faq.q: How can my dad find low-income senior apartments in Westchester?
faq.a: Search HousingSearch.ny.gov for HCR-financed properties, call the county's Section 8 administrator (CVR New York Westchester HCVP, applicant inquiries 914-873-1045) when its list is open, and ask the Westchester Department of Senior Programs and Services and local housing authorities for senior building lists.

faq.q: How long is the wait for NYCHA senior housing?
faq.a: NYCHA says it cannot estimate when you will be called because the waitlist is very large and vacancies are low. Applicants who live or work in New York City are prioritized. Keep the application current and renew it every two years.

faq.q: What is the income limit for Section 202 senior housing?
faq.a: Section 202 is for very low-income households, and HUD says household income must be less than 50% of the area median income where the property is. The dollar limit depends on the county and household size, and rent is typically 30% of adjusted income. Ask the property's manager for its current limits.

faq.q: Is a 55+ community the same as assisted living in New York?
faq.a: No. A 55+ community is regular housing that meets federal age rules, such as at least 80% of units having an occupant 55 or older. Adult homes and assisted living are licensed by the state, overseen by the Department of Health, and provide meals, personal care and supervision.

faq.q: Can I apply for both NYCHA public housing and Section 8?
faq.a: Yes. NYCHA lets you apply for both, but you can only receive one at a time. If you are selected for one, your priority on the other list is significantly reduced. HCR's Section 8 lists are separate and require their own application.
